questions.q: Why doesn't col("passenger_count") == None correctly find null rows?
options: Spark follows SQL's three-valued logic, where a comparison against null isn't 'equal' in the way == would suggest — .isNull()/.isNotNull() are the correct methods
It works perfectly and is the recommended approach
Because None doesn't exist as a concept in PySpark at all
Because == only works on string columns, never numeric ones
questions.explain: This is a real, common trap — .isNull() and .isNotNull() are built specifically to handle this correctly.

questions.q: What does trips.na.drop() do without any arguments?
options: Drops a row if ANY column in it is null
Drops a row only if EVERY column in it is null
Does nothing unless a subset is specified
Deletes the entire DataFrame
questions.explain: This can be too aggressive on a wide table — subset= narrows it to just the columns that matter for the task at hand.

Replaces every null value in the entire DataFrame with 0
Deletes every row where passenger_count is null
Converts the passenger_count column to a string type
questions.explain: na.fill() takes a default value per-type and only replaces nulls in the column(s) named in subset.

questions.q: Where do the nulls covered in this lesson actually come from earlier in the chapter?
options: Lesson 47's unmatched when() conditions and Lesson 48's failed .cast() calls both produce nulls silently, with no error
Nulls only ever come from the original source file, never from any PySpark operation
PySpark generates random nulls on every read for testing purposes
Nulls can only be introduced manually via na.fill()
questions.explain: This lesson is where you actually go looking for those silently-created nulls and decide what to do about them.

questions.q: Why might filling a missing fare_amount with 0 be worse than dropping that row entirely?
options: Because filling it with 0 would quietly corrupt any later aggregation, like a sum or average, over fare_amount
Filling with 0 is always the correct choice for every numeric column
Dropping rows is never appropriate under any circumstances
0 is not a valid value to pass to na.fill()
questions.explain: There's no universal right answer — it depends on what the null actually represents for that specific column.
